plan.title: AP Biology: Cells, Energy & Inheritance
plan.hook: Connect membrane transport, enzymes and inheritance in a focused AP-level introduction. This sampler is not a complete AP course or an official College Board resource.

sections.heading: A boundary that does useful work
sections.body:
A cell membrane is selectively permeable. Small nonpolar molecules can cross its lipid interior readily; ions generally need suitable transport proteins. A boundary is useful because it can maintain different conditions inside and outside a cell.

Diffusion produces net movement down a concentration gradient. Facilitated diffusion uses a channel or carrier to move material down its electrochemical gradient without directly spending cellular energy. A protein-assisted process is not automatically active transport. At equilibrium, molecules still move; opposing flows balance.

Osmosis is water movement across a selectively permeable membrane. With equal initial pressure, water tends to move toward the side with more solute that cannot cross. A cell in a hypertonic solution therefore initially loses water. Pressure and solute permeability matter: “water always follows any solute” is too broad. In a tissue experiment, keep temperature and exposure time fixed while varying the surrounding solution.
sections.visual: Picture two rooms joined by water-sized doors. One contains more large particles that cannot cross. Water shifts toward the particle-rich side until pressures balance.

questions.q: Has diffusion stopped when opposing flows become equal?
questions.hint: Separate molecular movement from net movement.
questions.answer: No. Random molecular motion continues, while equal opposing flows give no net concentration change.

sections.heading: Lower the barrier, keep the destination
sections.body:
A reaction can be energetically favourable yet slow. Reactants must pass through a transition state, and the activation barrier limits how frequently they succeed. An enzyme supplies a pathway with a lower barrier, increasing reaction rate under suitable conditions.

Catalysis does not change the overall free-energy difference or shift equilibrium. It speeds the approach to equilibrium, and the enzyme is regenerated during each catalytic cycle. Its molecular shape and environment matter: pH or temperature changes can alter activity, and sufficiently disruptive conditions can damage its structure.

ATP hydrolysis can help drive another process when the reactions are mechanistically coupled and the combined free-energy change is favourable. Breaking a bond alone costs energy; the energy balance belongs to the complete reaction. Likewise, a flattening rate curve at high substrate concentration can reflect occupied enzyme active sites, not an enzyme that has “run out of energy.”
sections.visual: Picture two valleys connected by a high mountain pass. An enzyme opens a lower pass between the same valleys. It changes the rate, not the destination height.

questions.q: Would adding an enzyme make an unfavourable reaction favourable?
questions.hint: Compare the barrier with the difference between endpoints.
questions.answer: No. Catalysis changes the rate, not the reaction’s overall free-energy difference or equilibrium position.

sections.heading: Count alleles before predicting traits
sections.body:
At a diploid locus, an individual generally has two alleles, one inherited from each parent. In a simple Mendelian model, an Aa parent produces A and a gametes with equal probability. For an Aa × Aa cross, the four equally likely combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa.

Combining Aa and aA gives a genotype ratio of 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. With complete dominance, AA and Aa share the dominant phenotype, producing a 3:1 phenotype ratio. Dominance concerns expression in a heterozygote; it does not mean an allele is common, beneficial or stronger.

For independent offspring under the same model, the probability that two offspring are both aa is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. A previous outcome does not force the next. Extending multiplication to different genes requires justified independence: linked loci and other biological complications can violate the simplest classroom assumptions.
sections.visual: Picture a two-by-two grid with A and a across the top and down the side. Each square combines one allele from each parent — the Punnett square.

questions.q: Why does a 3:1 phenotype ratio not mean all dominant-looking offspring are AA?
questions.hint: Two different genotypes can have the same phenotype.
questions.answer: With complete dominance, both AA and Aa show the dominant phenotype. The genotype ratio is 1:2:1.

questions.q: At equal initial pressure, a cell meets a solution with more nonpenetrating solute outside. What is the initial net water movement?
questions.explain: Water initially moves outward toward the higher concentration of nonpenetrating solute. Water still moves both ways, but the net flow is outward.

questions.q: A channel lets ions travel down their electrochemical gradient without ATP use. What is this?
questions.explain: A protein-assisted downhill movement is facilitated diffusion. Protein involvement alone does not make transport active.

questions.q: What changes when an enzyme catalyses a reaction?
choices: The equilibrium constant at fixed temperature
The activation barrier along the pathway
questions.explain: The enzyme provides a lower-barrier route. It does not change the reaction endpoints or equilibrium constant at fixed temperature.

questions.q: Why might reaction rate level off as substrate rises with fixed enzyme concentration?
choices: The enzyme is a consumed fuel
questions.explain: Saturation limits how much additional substrate can increase the rate when available active sites are already occupied.

questions.q: In the stated Aa × Aa model, what fraction of offspring are heterozygous?
questions.explain: Two of the four equally likely allele combinations are heterozygous. The 3/4 value describes the dominant phenotype, not the heterozygous genotype.

questions.q: Two independent offspring from this cross are both aa with what probability?
questions.explain: Each has probability 1/4 of aa. Independence lets us multiply: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.
